overlap.title: Miriam and Aaron speak together but have different narrated outcomes
overlap.summary: Both challenge Moses; Miriam receives the described skin affliction and exclusion.
overlap.reasoning: The narrative does not report the same bodily punishment for Aaron. Explaining why by gender, leadership or priestly status adds an interpretation not explicitly supplied here.

overlap.title: Moses’ relatives and the in-law label
overlap.summary: KJV calls Hobab Moses’ father-in-law; ASV and WEB call him brother-in-law. Exodus names Reuel and Jethro, while Numbers calls Hobab Reuel’s son. The apparent family conflict depends on the kinship reading.
overlap.reasoning: If every in-law label denotes the same paternal relationship, the named father and son create tension. Reading Hobab as brother-in-law avoids that particular generation conflict; equating Jethro and Reuel as two names for one person is a possible explanation, not an explicit identification in these passages. Numbers’ punctuation alone does not prove which antecedent receives the label.
overlap.scope: This comparison is edition-sensitive. Do not claim all translations make Hobab the father-in-law, or that Kenite and Midianite must be mutually exclusive ethnic identities. No original-language semantic range or family genealogy is established solely from English translations. Alias and clan relationships remain interpretation questions. The Greek of Judges 1:16 names Jethro where the Hebrew and KJV name no one, so in the Greek book both Jethro (1:16) and Hobab (4:11) carry the same in-law word. Brenton’s English renders that Greek word “father-in-law” in both verses; the same Greek word is used for the woman’s father at Judges 19:9, so it does not by itself fix the relationship. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.

checks.overlapDecision: Reviewed overlapping records and all ENTRIES studies: different finding, not duplicate.

overlap.title: A day with delayed sunset
overlap.summary: A literal extra day before sunset departs from ordinary Earth rotation. The account gives no physical mechanism; reading the battle language as poetry changes what is being assessed.
overlap.reasoning: Ordinary apparent daily solar motion is associated with Earth rotation; merely describing the Sun as moving is not the discrepancy. The issue is a literal extension of daylight beyond that cycle, which is not explained by ordinary rotation. The passage cites Jasher and contains elevated battle language, making interpretation relevant.
overlap.scope: This conditional comparison does not show Earth stopped rotating, calculate physical consequences, identify a historical date, or disprove supernatural intervention. NASA supplies the ordinary physical model, not a reconstruction of this battle. A figurative reading does not assert the same physical event.

overlap.title: The Midian account includes captive executions and distribution of survivors
overlap.summary: The narrative orders killings after capture and includes surviving female captives in the distribution of spoils.
overlap.reasoning: These are distinct claims: battlefield deaths, subsequent captive killings, distribution and absence of losses on one side. The latter does not make the campaign bloodless.
overlap.scope: The text supplies no individual culpability for each child, consent of captives or independent casualty verification. It does not specify the later treatment of every survivor; the ethical questions remain.
